body: Based on prior experience, try it with Python 3.6, and if that fails, 3.5.
Ping for updates on this, as far as I am aware the scripting system prefers Python 3.6, and may not work properly with other versions. Is this issue still present with 3.6?

Not checked recently, I'll try ASAP (not sure exactly when I have time for this). But TBH, I'm not sure I have an easy way of testing this with other Python versions. 

The problem here is not a problem due to the version of the Python executable, it's a problem with how the embedded python interpreter is built in obs. Since I'm building these from debian's package (dget + dpkg-buildpackage), I gave a quick look at patches in the debian source package, and there are a few patches in there that could be related, (e.g. there is a potential culprit in there, 0002-Hide-internal-symbols.patch, that adds a few `visibility=hidden` flags to compile commands), but rebuilding the package without these patches did not help. 

I've filled a bug on debian's tracker in the mean time. I'll keep you in touch here when I have feedback.

See https://bugs.debian.org/cgi-bin/bugreport.cgi?bug=958966
I've been fighting with this bug all weekend. I can't say I've made any progress. But I would love to see it fixed.

I've had cython modules fail to load with both Python 3.7 and Python 3.8.
I'm building the source at head with no additional patches.

I've found some bugs in the CMake modules that handle the SWIG bindings, Specifically that all but the last of the SWIG flags is overwritten here (https://github.com/obsproject/obs-studio/blob/master/deps/obs-scripting/obspython/CMakeLists.txt#L31-L36). But fixing that simply caused more build failures.

I'm really confused by how the python libraries are loaded on linux. They're dynamically loaded, but ,unlike Windows and Mac, on Linux we don't force load the symbols from the python library?

Just curious: Would @EricWF bugfix also solve the problem where trying to do something like `import ssl` results in `ImportError: /usr/lib/python3.8/lib-dynload/_ssl.cpython-38-x86_64-linux-gnu.so: undefined symbol: PyExc_OSError`.  They *seem* like they're the same problem but I'm not sure.

I can say for certain that the version of Python installed on my system (3.8.2) is the exact same version output when running `import platform; print(platform.python_version())` in an OBS Python script.
@riskable it's the same problem indeed, so if the fix provided by @EricWF works, it should also allow you to import ssl (or any other binary module).

> OK. So I resolved the issue by changing `os_dlopen`
> 
> ```
> -       void *res = dlopen(dylib_name.array, RTLD_LAZY);
> +       void *res = dlopen(dylib_name.array, RTLD_LAZY | RTLD_DEEPBIND | RTLD_GLOBAL);
> ```
> 
> Just adding RTLD_GLOBAL caused some other things to break.

I was encountering similar errors with modules such as `math` which contain native code. I can confirm that the patch proposed by @EricWF is sufficient to fix the problem on my install as well. The line to be changed is located [here](https://github.com/obsproject/obs-studio/blob/bb890a674e8289f7be2825fbeea13c7d2f9623af/libobs/util/platform-nix.c#L74).

body: I appreciate the efforts of all the people here who have validated this fix. Please be sure to post in the PR that implements this change (#3335) which distro & Python version you were using when this change solved your issue.

> I'm really confused by how the python libraries are loaded on linux. They're dynamically loaded, but ,unlike Windows and Mac, on Linux we don't force load the symbols from the python library?

https://bugs.python.org/issue21536

Every importable module implemented in C, even the stdlib ones, no longer links to libpython but expects the interpreter to provide the needed global symbols on python >=3.8

obs-studio does not directly link to libpython, but uses dlopen, then marks it as non-global despite trying to embed a standard python interpreter. This then breaks every consumer of the embedded interpreter.

issue.title: [Linux] Cannot load url-text.py plugin

repository.name: obs-studio
repository.description: OBS Studio - Free and open source software for live streaming and screen recording

issue.body:
## Platform

Operating system and version: Arch Linux
OBS Studio version:  OBS Studio - 25.0.8-2 (linux)

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open the scripts dialog
2. Click add
3. Select url-text.py
4. Open the Script log


The following error comes up:


```
[url-text.py] Traceback (most recent call last):
[url-text.py]   File "/usr/share/obs/obs-plugins/frontend-tools/scripts/url-text.py", line 2, in <module>
[url-text.py]     import urllib.request
[url-text.py]   File "/usr/lib/python3.8/urllib/request.py", line 84, in <module>
[url-text.py]     import base64
[url-text.py]   File "/usr/lib/python3.8/base64.py", line 10, in <module>
[url-text.py]     import struct
[url-text.py]   File "/usr/lib/python3.8/struct.py", line 13, in <module>
[url-text.py]     from _struct import *
[url-text.py] ImportError: /usr/lib/python3.8/lib-dynload/_struct.cpython-38-x86_64-linux-gnu.so: undefined symbol: _PyFloat_Pack4
```

I believe the problem is OBS specific as if I just create a python script `test.py` with 

```
 import urllib.request
```

and run it from the command line `python test.py`, I don't get this error. It seems to be to do with the way OBS runs the python script. 

Unfortunately, googling "undefined symbol: _PyFloat_Pack4" doesn't give any meaningful results.

body:
> then marks it as non-global despite trying to embed a standard python interpreter.

To be clear obs just links it like every other system would link a normal library. It is not marked non-global, it is left unspecified.

> This then breaks everywhere.

This is better rephrased as, and then python broke linking normally for everyone.

> To be clear obs just links it like every other system would link a normal library. It is not marked non-global, it is left unspecified.

It doesn't *link* at all, since dlopen != link, hence the problem. :p Obeying default semantics still means the dlopen call site is saying "yes, gimme some non-global".

It's not intuitive that this should suddenly start breaking *now*, but technically it would probably feel more correct to do so either way in order to better act like a drop-in replacement for libpython, and other language interpreters sometimes behaved this way from the beginning rather than suddenly changing like python did in 3.8.

> This is better rephrased as, and then python broke linking normally for everyone.

That may be so, but my intention was to clarify that it breaks every part of the embedded interpreter e.g. wide swaths of the stdlib.

Nothing to do with which type of projects get broken or whose "fault" it is.

From the bug provided, the modules were compiled to support the obs use case explicitly "where the interpreter is linked with a library dlopened by an embedding application (I suppose for some kind of plugin system)". And were subsequently broken because "IHMO it's a bad usage of dlopen()". I mean its pretty clear phrasing to me.

--edit
and their follow-up to making this decision:
"bpo-21536 basically broke the compilation of all applications which embed Python." for the icing on top.

[`ctypes`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/ctypes.html) and [`cffi`](https://pypi.org/project/cffi/) also fail to load with `ImportError ... undefined symbol ... `. 
- python3.8 , ubuntu 20.04
